To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
two novel mutations were identified, which led to considerable differences in clinical and beating ciliary phenotype.

two novel, likely pathogenic mutations in the DNA H11 gene in the DNAH 11 gene were detected in two families with primary ciliary dyskenia (PCD), which showed considerable variation in the ciliary beating phenotype and disease severity.
Two novel mutations in the Dyinein Arm Heavy Chain (DNAH11 gene) were found in two unrelated, Finnish primary ciliary dyskinetic families.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the clinical and genetic heterogeneity of PCD, and the importance of the ciliary beating pattern in PCD diagnosis.
the importance of early diagnosis and treatment of PCD to prevent irreversible damage to the respiratory tract.
the clinical phenotype of DNAH11 related PCD and we hope to contribute to the understanding of this disease and its management.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
PCD is an important differential diagnosis in children with chronic and repeatedly treated wet and dry cough.
the DNAH11 mutation is associated with PCD, but the phenotype of the disease can vary from severe to mild.
the DNAH11 mutation can lead to a wide spectrum of clinical and beating ciliopathy phenotypes, which is why it is necessary to perform a detailed analysis in the diagnostic process.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
PCD should be suspected in children with a chronic wet cough.
PCD is not a rare disease in Finland.
the diagnosis of PCD should be made by experienced specialists and that the diagnosis should be based on clinical symptoms, ciliary movement analysis and molecular genetic testing.
The main takeaway from our work is that
DNAH11 gene mutations can be associated with a variety of ciliary beating patterns and disease severity.
PCD can have considerable variation in clinical and ciliary beating pattern, and that it is necessary to update data-bases and diagnostic guidelines for PCD to keep up with new mutations.
the clinical picture of PCD may vary greatly, even within the same family, and that the phenotype is not necessarily a good indicator of disease severity.
